source_text: Occurrit disceptatio, an etiam hoc ab excessu statim fiat, an quasdam animas aliqua ratio detineat hic interim, an etiam receptas liceat postea ab inferis ex arbitrio vel ex imperio interve nire: nec harum enim opinionum suasoriae desunt. Creditum est, insepultos non ante ad inferos redigi, quam justa perceperint, secundum homericum Patroclum funus in somnis de Achille flagitantem, quod non alias adire portas inferum posset, arcentibus eum longe animabus sepultorum. Novimus autem, praeter poetica jura, pietatis quoque homericae industriam. Tanto magis enim curam sepulturae collocavit, quanto etiam moram ejus injuriosam animabus incusavit; simul et ne quis defunctum domi detinens ipse amplius cum illo maceretur enormitate solatii dolore nutriti. Ita querelas animae insepultae ad utrumque conficit; ut instantia funeris, et honor corporum servetur, et moeror adfectuum temperetur. Caeterum, quam vanum ut anima corporis justa sustineat, quasi aliquid ex illis ad inferos avehat? Multo vanius, si injuria deputabitur animae cessatio sepulturae, quam pro gratia deberet amplecti. Utique enim tardius ad inferos abstrahi malet, quae nec mori voluit. Amabit impium haeredem, per quem adhuc pascitur luce: aut si qua pro certo injuria est tardius sub terram detrudi, titulus autem injuriae cessatio est sepulturae, per quam iniquum eam injuria adfici, cui non imputabitur cessatio sepulturae, ad proximos scilicet pertinens. Aiunt et immatura morte praevenras eousque vagari isthic, donec reliquatio compleatur aetatum, quas tum pervixissent, si non intempestive obiissent. Porro, aut constituta sunt tempora unicuique, et constituta praeripi posse non credam; aut si constituta sunt quidem, Dei tamen voluntate vel aliqua potestate mutilantur, frustra mutilantur, si jam impleti sustinent; aut si non sunt constituta, nulla erit reliquatio temporum non constitutorum. Adhuc addam: ecce obiit (verbi gratia) infans sub uberum fontibus, puta nunc puer investis, puta vesticeps, qui tamen octoginta annos victurus fuisset: hos praereptos ut anima ejus hic post mortem transigat, quale est? Aetatem enim non potest capere sine corpore; quia per corpora operantur aetates. Nostri autem illud quoque recogitent, corpora eadem recepturas in resurrectione animas, in quibus decesserunt. Iidem ergo sperabuntur et corporum modi, et eaedem aetates quae corporum modos faciunt. Quo ergo pacto potest infantis anima hic transigere praerepta tempora, ut octogenaria resurgat in corpore mensis unius? Aut si hic necesse erit ea tempora impleri quae fuerant destinata, num et ordinem vitae quam sortita sunt tempora pariter cum illis hic destinatum, pariter hic anima decurret, ut et studeat ab infantia, pueritiae delegata; et militet ab adolescentia, juventae excitata; et censeat a juventa, senectae ponderata; et foenus exprimat et agrum urgeat, naviget, litiget, nubat, laboret, aegritudines obeat; et quaecumque illam cum temporibus manebant tristia ac laeta? Sed haec sine corpore quomodo transigentur? vita sine vita? Sed vacua erunt tempora, solo decursu adimplenda. Quid ergo prohibet apud inferos ea impleri, ubi perinde nullus est usus illorum? Ita dicimus omnem animam, quaqua aetate decesserit, in ea stare ad eum diem, usque perfectum illud repromittitur ad angelicae plenitudinis mensuram temperatum. Proinde nec extorres inferum habebuntur, quas vi ereptas arbitrantur, praecipue per atrocitates suppliciorum, crucis dico, et securis, et gladii, et ferae; nec isti porro exitus violenti, quos justitia decernit, violentiae vindex. «Et ideo, inquies, scelestae quaeque animae inferis exulant.» Alterum ergo constituas compello, aut bonos inferos, aut malos. Si malos placet, et jam praecipitari illuc animae pessimae debent. Si bonos, cur idem, animas immaturas, et innuptas, pro conditione aetatis puras et innocuas, interim dignas inferis non judicas?
thought_title: The State of the Soul After Death
pass_a_gloss: A dispute arises, whether the soul also immediately comes into being from excess, or whether some reason detains certain souls here in the meantime, or whether it is also permitted for souls that have been received to intervene again from the lower world by choice or by command: for there are not lacking persuasive arguments for these opinions. It has been believed that those not buried are not led to the lower world before they have received the proper rites, according to the Homeric funeral of Patroclus, who in dreams begged Achilles, because he was not able to approach the gates of the lower world otherwise, the souls of the buried keeping him at a distance. We know, however, beyond poetic laws, also the industriousness of Homeric piety; for it placed such great care on burial, because it also accused the harmful delay of the souls; at the same time, so that no one, keeping the deceased at home, might himself be tormented by excessive grief, nourished by the pain of sorrow. Thus, the complaints of the unburied soul are settled on both sides; so that the urgency of the funeral, and the honor of the bodies may be preserved, and the sorrow of the emotions may be tempered. Moreover, how empty it is that the soul should sustain the proper rites of the body, as if it were to carry something from them to the lower world? Much more empty, if the cessation of burial is imputed as an injury to the soul, which ought to be accepted with gratitude. For certainly, it prefers to be more slowly drawn away to the lower world, which did not wish to die. It will love the impious heir, through whom it is still nourished by the light; or if there is some certain injury, it is more slowly cast under the earth, the title of the injury being the cessation of burial, through which the unjust soul is afflicted by the injury, to which the cessation of burial is not imputed, pertaining to those nearest. They say that those who have been prevented by an immature death wander about there until the remainder of their ages is completed, which they would have attained if they had not died prematurely. Furthermore, either the times have been established for each, and I do not believe that they can be taken away; or if they have been established, they are nevertheless mutilated by the will of God or some power, they are mutilated in vain, if they have already been fulfilled; or if they have not been established, there will be no remainder of non-established times. I will add this: behold, an infant has died under the fountains of the breast, suppose now a boy invested, suppose a youth clothed, who nevertheless would have lived eighty years: how can its soul transact the times that have been taken away here after death? For it cannot grasp age without a body; because ages operate through bodies. Our people must also consider this, that the same bodies will receive the souls in the resurrection, in which they departed. Therefore, the same modes of bodies, and the same ages that make the modes of bodies, will be hoped for. In what way, therefore, can the soul of an infant transact the times that have been taken away here, so that it may rise again in the body of one month old as an eighty-year-old? Or if it is necessary here to fill up the times that were destined, will the soul also run through the order of life that was allotted to it, together with those times, here; so that it may study from infancy, delegated to childhood; and serve from adolescence, excited to youth; and judge from youth, weighed down by old age; and exact interest and urge on the field, navigate, litigate, marry, labor, endure illnesses; and whatever sad and happy things remained with it and the times? But how can these things be transacted without a body? Life without life? But the times will be empty, to be fulfilled by mere passing. What, therefore, prevents these things from being fulfilled in the lower world, where there is just as much use of them? Thus, we say that every soul, whatever age it departed, stands in it until that day, when the perfect thing is promised, tempered to the measure of angelic fullness. Therefore, those will not be considered strangers to the lower world, whom they think have been violently torn away, especially through the atrocities of punishments, I say, of the cross, and the axe, and the sword, and the wild beast; nor will these violent exits, which justice decrees, be avenged by violence. And so, you say, every wicked soul is banished from the lower world. You must establish another thing, either good or evil lower world. If evil, the worst souls ought to be cast down there already. If good, why do you not judge the same, immature souls, and unmarried, pure and innocent according to the condition of age, worthy of the lower world in the meantime?
